title: Paloma and the Typewriter
premise: In the winter of 1918, Odile Vane — a widowed lighthouse keeper living quietly as a man, as he has for fifteen years — finds a drowned courier's satchel washed ashore, containing documents proving a local armistice profiteer orchestrated the bridge sabotage that stranded the island. Cut off from the mainland by the season's closing storms, Odile must move the evidence through the island's three checkpoints: the harbor master, the garrison, and the telegraph office — each guarded by someone who knows him by a different name. With help from the found family of the village inn, he smuggles the truth out by sea before the armistice is signed, at the cost of revealing who he truly is.
about_author: W. M. Brightwater is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing lighthouse logs from the North Atlantic. Their fiction explores the quiet heroism of people history forgot to record.

chapters.title: The Last Ferry
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. On the final day before the bridge closes, Odile declines passage to the mainland, choosing his solitary routine over the mainland doctor who suspects his secret. The ferry leaves without him. Emotional beat: the comfort and cost of chosen isolation.

chapters.title: Salt and Lamplight
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Establishes the lighthouse rhythm: trimming wicks, logging weather, the ritual that keeps grief and identity at bay. He writes letters to his late wife on the typewriter she left him, never sent. Emotional beat: tender melancholy, a man at peace on the surface.

chapters.title: What the Sea Gave Back
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, storm night. A courier's body washes into the rocks below the light; Odile retrieves the satchel — sealed orders implicating shipping magnate Corvel in the bridge sabotage. He nearly burns it, but the courier's face stays with him. Emotional beat: dread and reluctant responsibility.

chapters.title: The Inn at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. He seeks shelter from a squall at the village inn and is absorbed, unasked, into its orbit: landlady Marta, her orphaned niece Paloma, and shell-shocked veteran Tomas. They feed him before he can refuse. Emotional beat: the warmth of found family, resisted.

chapters.title: Checkpoint One: The Harbor Master
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The harbor master, an old friend of his late wife, mentions the drowned courier and offers a reward for 'lost papers.' Odile lies smoothly — too smoothly — and realizes Corvel's reach already touches the island. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Paloma
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Twelve-year-old Paloma, who idolizes the lighthouse keeper, follows him home and discovers the satchel. She doesn't ask what's inside; she asks to help. Emotional beat: unexpected alliance; Odile's loneliness cracks.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Papers
chapters.summary: Shared POV. Odile and Marta decode the documents: Corvel sabotaged the bridge to delay the armistice and inflate shipping contracts. Marta's son died on a delayed relief ship. Her grief turns to purpose. Emotional beat: private loss becomes shared cause.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, flashback chapter. Fifteen years earlier: how Odile became Odile, burying his old name with his wife's help, and why the lighthouse was the only place a person could vanish and still be useful. Emotional beat: the weight of the secret, fully revealed.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Two: The Garrison
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas, who sweeps the garrison floor, learns a patrol will search the lighthouse at week's end. His loyalty splits between the army that broke him and the people who took him in. Emotional beat: a broken man choosing his family over his uniform.

chapters.title: Hiding the Light
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The search comes early. Odile hides the satchel inside the lens housing while soldiers question him, and the garrison captain studies his papers a moment too long. Paloma's chatter saves him. Emotional beat: near-exposure; the noose tightens.

chapters.title: Corvel Comes Ashore
chapters.summary: Corvel's POV. The magnate arrives to oversee the island's 'relief effort,' charming the garrison and buying the harbor master outright. He notices the lighthouse keeper who won't look at him. Emotional beat: the banality of corruption, and the hunter's instinct.

chapters.title: The Typewriter Speaks
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma finds Odile's unsent letters to his wife and learns his secret. Instead of betrayal, she types him a letter of her own: 'I know, and it changes nothing.' Emotional beat: acceptance; the deepest bond of the book.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three: The Telegraph Office
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Marta bribes the telegraph clerk with Corvel's own counterfeit ledger, but the clerk warns that all outgoing wires are now read aloud to Corvel. The island is a closed fist. Emotional beat: hope narrowing to a single channel.

chapters.title: The Storm That Wouldn't End
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A week of hurricane-force storms; the light must be kept burning or ships will founder — including, Odile realizes, the boat they'll need. He keeps the watch alone for three nights. Emotional beat: endurance; duty as identity.

chapters.title: What Tomas Carried Back
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas deserts to scout the cove where a fishing boat might be launched, and is caught by Corvel's men. He gives up nothing but comes back changed, knowing the price of failure now has a face. Emotional beat: sacrifice and its quiet cost.

chapters.title: The Bargain at the Inn
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Corvel visits the inn, offers Odile passage off the island in exchange for 'whatever the sea gave him.' Odile serves him tea and lies to his face, understanding Corvel suspects but cannot prove. Emotional beat: the hunter and the keeper, masked civility.

chapters.title: Paloma's Plan
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma proposes the impossible route: run the boat through the narrows during the armistice celebrations, when every checkpoint will be watching the bridge, not the water. The family argues, then commits. Emotional beat: the child becomes the strategist.

chapters.title: Armistice Eve
chapters.summary: Shared POV. The island prepares to celebrate a peace that may be signed on Corvel's terms. Odile oils the boat, seals the papers in oilcloth, and writes one last letter to his wife — this time signing his true name. Emotional beat: readiness; the secret set down.

chapters.title: The Narrows
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, climax. Odile and Paloma run the narrows through gunfire and breaking waves while Marta and Tomas stage a decoy fire at the garrison. The boat nearly founders; Paloma's small hands hold the tiller true. Emotional beat: terror, trust, and triumph at full pitch.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: Shared POV. The evidence reaches the armistice commission by dawn; Corvel is arrested as the ink dries on the true agreement. The island celebrates a peace it will never fully know it saved. Emotional beat: vindication, quiet and unclaimed.

chapters.title: The Name in the Logbook
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile returns to find the village waiting — not with suspicion but with the inn's spare room made up, his name already on the registry. He keeps the lighthouse, but no longer alone. Emotional beat: belonging, chosen and returned.

chapters.title: What Paloma Typed
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, coda. Years later, Paloma, now the lighthouse keeper's apprentice and heir, donates Odile's letters and logs to the mainland archive — the record history almost lost. The final letter, signed with his true name, is read aloud. Emotional beat: legacy; identity preserved by the family that kept it.
